  Guide to the City Commission Proceedings
The Oral Communication portion of the agenda is for members of the public to present items which are not listed on the
agenda, but are under the subject matter jurisdiction of the Commission. Although no action may be taken, the Commission
and staff will follow up, at an appropriate time, on those items needing response. Each speaker is limited to (3) three minutes.
Time may be surrendered by deferring (1) one minute to another speaker, not to exceed a total of (8) eight minutes. The
speaker wishing to defer time must be present when the item is heard. In order to be recognized and present an item, each
speaker must complete and submit to the Recording Secretary a Request to Speak form prior to the beginning of the item
being announced by the Chair (forms are available at the entrance to the meeting room). Speakers are taken in the order slips
are submitted.

Items in Consent Calendar Section A have already been considered by the Commission at a previous meeting where the
public was invited to comment, after which a decision was made. These items are not subject to public discussion at this
meeting because the vote taken at the previous meeting was final. Resolutions concerning decisions made at previous
meetings are for the purpose of memorializing the decision to assure the accuracy of the findings, the prior vote, and any
conditions imposed.

Items in Consent Calendar Section B have not been discussed previously by the Commission. If discussion is desired, an
item may be removed from the Consent Calendar for individual consideration. Commissioners may indicate a negative or
abstaining vote on any individual item by so declaring prior to the vote on the motion to adopt the entire Consent
Calendar. Items excluded from the Consent Calendar will be taken up by the Commission following the action on the Consent
Calendar. The Commission first will take up the items for which public speaker requests have been submitted. Public speakers
shall follow the rules as set forth under Oral Communication.

Old Business items have appeared on previous agendas but have either been continued or tabled to this meeting with no final
action having been taken. Public comment shall follow the rules as set forth under Oral Communication.

Items in New Business are items which are appearing for the first time for formal action. Public comment shall follow the
rules as set forth under Oral Communication.

Copies of the staff reports or other written documentation relating to each item of business described above are on file in the
Public Safety Department, Malibu City Hall, 23825 Stuart Ranch Road, Malibu, California and are available for public
inspection during regular office hours which are 7:30 a.m. to 5:30 p.m., Monday through Thursday, and 7:30 a.m. to 4:30
p.m., Friday. Written materials distributed to the Commission within 72 hours of the Commission meeting are available for
public inspection immediately upon distribution (Government Code Section 54957.5(b)(2). Copies of staff reports and written
materials may be purchased for $0.10 per page. Pursuant to State law, this agenda was posted at least 72 hours prior to the
meeting.

The City Hall phone number is (310) 456-2489. To contact City Hall using a telecommunication device for the deaf (TDD),
please call (800) 735-2929 and a California Relay Service operator will assist you. In compliance with the Americans with
Disabilities Act, if you need special assistance to participate in this meeting, please contact Yolanda Bundy, Environmental
Sustainability Director, at (310) 456-2489, ext. 229. Notification 48 hours prior to the meeting will enable the City to make
reasonable arrangements to ensure accessibility to this meeting. [28 CFR 35.102-35.104 ADD Title II].

Requests to show an audio or video presentation during a Commission meeting should be directed to the Media Team at
media@malibucity.org. Material must be submitted by 12:00 p.m. on the meeting day.

I hereby certify under penalty of perjury, under the laws of the State of California, that the foregoing agenda was posted in

ITEM 5  NEW BUSINESS

  A.  PCH Safety Review
  Recommended Action: 1) Receive a report from staff on the status of PCH Safety
  improvements, and 2) Provide feedback to staff.

  Public Safety Director Dueñas stated that she would brief the Commission on the
  status of improvements to Pacific Coast Highway (PCH) safety and law
  enforcement enhancement after Public Works Director DuBoux provided
  information on structural changes.

  Public Works Director Duboux provided a summary of planned improvements to
  PCH safety. He discussed the PCH Safety Study, approved by the City Council in
  June of 2015, which identified 130 projects. He stated that the City completed seven
  projects, 15 were in construction, 25 in the design stage, six in the planning stage,
  and 14 projects were identified to work on. He stated that Caltrans completed two,
  had one in construction, three in the design phase, and identified 45 additional tasks
  to pursue. He stated that two of the projects under construction were signal
  synchronization from Topanga Canyon Road to John Tyler Drive and the median
  project from John Tyler Drive to Puerco Canyon Road. He stated that in addition
  to signal synchronization, there were other enhancements planned which included
  red light cameras that detected speeding vehicles and changed the upcoming signal
  to a red light which forced drivers to stop. He stated that projects in the design phase
  included right-turn lane intersection improvements at Trancas Canyon Road, the
  pedestrian undercrossing at Corral Canyon Beach, median improvements at
  Paradise Cove and Zuma Beach, and crosswalk improvements at PCH and Big
  Rock Drive. He stated that the City collaborated with Caltrans on intersection
  improvements at PCH and Las Flores Canyon Road and Rambla Pacifico Street.
  He stated that projects in the planning stage would move forward when funding
  was available and included signal synchronization from John Tyler Drive to
  Trancas Canyon Road, pedestrian improvements at Paradise Cove, extension of the
  right-turn lane at Morning View Drive, and installation of a new median at
  Heathercliff Road. He stated additional tasks for the upcoming year included
  determining if the speed limit could be lowered, improved reflection and visibility
  of street name signs, new streetlights at Guernsey Avenue, Latigo Canyon Road,
  Encinal Canyon Road, and Matador Beach, relocation of bus stops near Kanan
  Dume Road and Webb Way, and considering realignment of Encinal Canyon Road
  and Malibu Canyon Road. He stated that completed projects included the PCH
  Parking Study, La Costa pedestrian improvements, the arrester bed at Kanan Dume
  Road, intersection improvements at Big Rock Drive, and increased law
  enforcement. He stated that there was not enough room for installation of a
  roundabout at Webb Way. He stated that the City and Caltrans collaborated on a

  list indicating the lead agency on projects and that coordination with them would
  continue.
  Public Safety Director Dueñas stated that the City Manager met with local elected
  leaders and the California Highway Patrol (CHP) prior to and since the fatality
  incident that occurred on October 17, 2023. She stated that immediate permission
  was given by the City to the Sheriff’s Department for overtime shifts for street
  racing operations and reported the prior Friday, 27 speeding citations were issued.
  She stated that a short-term overtime contract that included canyon operations with
  the CHP was in place while the longer-term contract for three dedicated officers
  was pursued. She stated that the City purchased six Lidar speed guns, four for use
  by Sheriff Deputies and two for use by the CHP. She stated that public education
  efforts increased, and a public safety website was launched on December 8, 2023
  with information on City activities and efforts by elected officials. She reported that
  speed ticket camera legislation for Malibu would be proposed and that support from
  the community was needed. She stated that a public relations firm was engaged for
  public education efforts to deter racing and unsafe driving.

  In response to Commissioner Gibbs, Public Safety Director Dueñas stated that
  initial public relations efforts were by a firm referred by the Joint Powers Authority
  Insurance (JPAI) to avoid the delay of the request for proposals (RFP) process, but
  an RFP would be conducted for any work needed beyond what the firm offered.

  In response to Ex Officio Member Woodworth, Public Works Director DuBoux
  stated that there was an understanding between the City and Caltrans of the lead
  agency on projects, they had a good plan moving forward, and he would stay in
  contact with them about priorities and action. He stated that there was collaboration
  between the agencies and that many projects required a City coastal development
  permit (CDP) which would be worked independently from coordination with
  Caltrans and approval time depended on the scope of the project.

  Ex Officio Member Woodworth encouraged the City to prioritize and expedite
  approval of projects that had the greatest impact on saving lives. He related his
  experience on the canyon roads where he encountered speeding and unsafe drivers
  in the evenings.

  In response to Commissioner Gibbs, Public Works Director DuBoux stated that the
  City took the lead on some projects, with the support of Caltrans and others Caltrans
  took the lead with collaboration with the City. He stated that projects impactful and
  important to the community could be suggested and pursued by the City.

  In response to Commissioner Merrick, Public Safety Director Dueñas stated that
  the three dedicated CHP officers could begin once the contract was signed, and
  their schedule coordinated with the Lost Hills Sheriff’s Department for maximum
  effectiveness and best use of resources based upon their expertise to avoid
  unnecessary redundancies. She stated that radar machines and license plate readers

  were two different things and the City had one license plate reader, of an eventual
  27, that would be operational with Southern California Edison’s cooperation.
  In response to Commissioner Merrick, Public Works Director DuBoux stated that
  the City would explore whether K-Rails or fencing could be implemented into the
  Corral Canyon Beach undercrossing.

  In response to Chair Chris Frost, Public Safety Director Dueñas stated that the City
  purchased six Lidar guns in addition to the four that were purchased two years prior
  and she would verify their location with the Sheriff’s Department. She stated that
  an emblem distinguishing the license plate car as Malibu’s was on hold until the
  substation opened, but she could explore expediting it.

  Commissioner Frost stated years prior, a deputy took the car to Chatsworth and
  Deputy Mike Treinen located it and brought it back to Malibu. He discussed the
  impact of having a no-call traffic car patrolling four nights per week until 3:00 a.m.,
  CHP presence, and more radar guns had on PCH safety. He commented that
  spreading the message on social media that vehicles would be impounded for 30
  days and incur thousands of dollars in expense would deter racing.

  In response to Commissioner Gibbs, Public Safety Director Dueñas stated that the
  Lidar guns the City funded would only be used in Malibu and would be outfitted
  with tracking devices and agreed the guns were effective.

  In response to Chair Frost, Public Safety Director Dueñas stated that all equipment,
  including the electronic ticket writers and the car should be tracked. She stated that
  the two license plate reading cameras at Malibu Canyon Road were a couple of
  months from being hardwired. She stated that recently passed speed camera
  legislation prohibited installation on State Highways and new legislation would be
  introduced but she did not know who was writing the bill. She stated that close
  attention would be paid and the legislation needed grassroots community support.

  In response to Chair Frost, Public Works Director DuBoux stated that there was
  more communication between Caltrans staff in recent weeks than previously and
  that they were supportive in the positive collaboration, and he would continue to
  press them to prioritize and address the City’s concerns about PCH safety.

  Chair Frost commented that there was an electronic message board, but no speed
  limit signs for construction approaching Corral Canyon Road westbound. He stated
  that the Trancas Canyon Road area was improved by more signage and lighting.

  In response to Chair Frost, Public Works Director DuBoux stated that Caltrans
  planned to resurface the eastbound lane for glare reduction caused by the crack-seal
  repairs, and Caltrans was seeking additional funding.

  Public Safety Director Duenas reported that City Council would receive a
  presentation on January 22, 2024 on the School Safety Report, with members of
  the school board present. She stated that an executive summary would be posted on
  the City’s website. She stated that the City met with the school district in December
  2023 who indicated that the contents of the report would be conveyed to each
  school and their Parent Teacher Association. She reported that the City worked with
  the Las Virgenes-Malibu Council of Governments on the update to the hazard
  notification plan which would be posted on the City’s website for a two-week
  public comment period before it was taken to City Council for adoption. She stated
  that she expected the update of the Emergency Operations Plan soon for review and
  would invite the Commission to provide comments.

  Public Safety Liaison Flores reported that the contract with The People Concern for
  homelessness outreach and the contract for parking enforcement services would
  end the current fiscal year and a new RFP would be issued in the coming days. He
  stated that they were working on establishing the temporary impound yard at
  Malibu High School for the summer. He announced the 2024 Homeless Count
  would be held January 24, 2024, and invited interested volunteers to register online.
  He announced a virtual homelessness community meeting would be held January
  17, 2024 with the meeting link available on the Homelessness Information page on
  the City’s website. He stated that it was expected the application packet for the
  automated license plate recognition (ALPR) cameras would be submitted that
  week, and once approved, installation could commence.

  Emergency Services Coordinator Flores provided highlights from Public Safety
  events in November and December 2023. She stated that the November 9, 2023
  open house at City Hall featured Public Safety Department staff, representatives
  from the Los Angeles County Fire Department (LACFD), Los Angeles Sheriff
  Department (LASD), Community Emergency Response Team (CERT), Volunteers
  on Patrol, and Arson Watch. She stated that on November 9, 2023, Public Safety
  Director Dueñas and Fire Safety Liaison Brad Yocum participated in an interview
  with KNBC and KCAL and discussed the Emergency Operations Center (EOC)
  and community disaster preparedness. She reported that on November 16, 2023,
  EOC training for all staff was held and explained that EOC activation occurred
  during large-scale disasters that required a high level of coordination. She stated
  that December 6 and 7, 2023, the City conducted a disaster scenario-based EOC
  exercise for all staff with realistic EOC activation. She announced June 2024 Public
  Safety Expo preparations were underway and they were exploring expanding the
  event. She announced additional EOC training would be conducted in the coming
  months utilizing the newly implemented EOC software system. She announced
  CERT classes would be conducted at City Hall from April 18, 2024 to May 30,
  2024 and that registration information was available on the City’s website.

  Fire Safety Liaison Vandermeulen provided an update on the Subdivision Review
  Program, a result of Assembly Bill 2911, where Cal Fire identified communities
  and subdivisions of 30 or more homes with only one access/egress point. He stated

  that LACFD Fire Prevention Division identified several Malibu communities: Big
  Rock, Rambla Orienta, Principio (Malibu West), upper Trancas, Carral Canyon
  where access/egress was through Malibu, Carbon Canyon, Winding Way, Murphy
  Way / Ramirez Canyon, and Latigo Shores. He reported that the $200,000 Cal Fire
  grant application was due on Wednesday, January 10, 2024 for funding toward

  community outreach, and an RFP for a consultant. He discussed the 2024 Fire Risk
  Reduction Community list and stated that the application period opened December
  1, 2023 and closed in April 2024. He stated that it identified communities that took
  proactive approaches to wildfire resilience efforts and part of the requirement was
  addressing the Subdivision Review Program mitigation recommendations. He
  stated that grant priority was given to those pursuing a grant to become a Fire Risk
  Reduction Community. He stated that appearing on that list demonstrated that the
  community was proactive with wildfire resilience and provided additional grant
  funding opportunities.

  In response to Commissioner Merrick, Fire Safety Liaison Vandermeulen
  confirmed that the criteria were 30 properties with one access / egress. He stated
  that he would research how condominiums were factored, and whether Bailard
  Road fit the criteria. He stated that the main idea was for evacuation of the long,
  winding, narrow, miles-long canyon roads was addressed. He stated that they had
  a good working relationship with the captain responsible for Malibu for Land Use
  Planning for Cal Fire, who was receptive and open to suggestions for additional
  neighborhoods.

  Fire Safety Liaison Bradley Yocum discussed Firewise Communities and reported
  Big Rock Mesa and Malibu Country Estates were in good standing. He stated that
  four were pending, and they conducted risk analysis and assessment for Malibu
  West, which was sent to the State for review. He reported that approximately 70
  wildfire assessments were conducted in 2023 and encouraged residents to form a
  Firewise Community. He stated although there had to be eight to 2400 dwelling
  units for qualification, exceptions were made to include Topanga and North of
  Topanga which exceeded the limit. He stated that they worked with the LACFD
  Forestry Division, Cal Fire, and LACFD, and City Fire Safety Liaisons were now
  allowed to conduct risk analysis and assessments. He stated that the Forestry
  Division conducted assessments outside of the Malibu city limits.

  In response to Commissioner Gibbs, Fire Safety Liaison Yocum stated that risk
  assessments were similar to home wildfire assessments, but on a larger scale for the
  community itself. He stated that assessments included the number of roofs that were
  Class A, homes with closed box eaves, stucco, and home hardening measures
  undertaken. He stated that depending on the community, they drove or walked
  through the neighborhood, or both, to get a feel for the area and talk to residents.
  He stated that not all homes participated, but intel was compiled, and a report
  composed on a sampling. He stated that Cal Fire and the Forestry Division wanted
  an update every five years and a three-year action plan was developed based on the

  five-year assessment, which included recommendations, mitigation measures, and
  an educational component. He stated that a core group of interested residents
  managed and maintained activities and that Malibu residents were interested in
  preparations for the next fire. He discussed the City’s participation in the Santa
  Monica Mountains Regional Fire Safe Council, which included members from the
  Resource Conservation District in Topanga. He stated that they were pursuing
  501(c)(3) status to apply for funding and grants for personnel. He stated that initial

  Supervisor Lindsey Horvath’s office. He stated that it was progressive in that
  commitment from communities from Chatworth to the coast was sought.

  In response to Commissioner Merrick, Fire Safety Liaison Yocum stated that
  efforts would be made to bring residents together for program participation in areas
  not covered by a Homeowners Association. He stated that to remain active,
  documentation proving one hour per home, per year was spent on efforts to firesafe
  each participating home. He provided the example of 30 participating homes would
  need documentation for 30 hours annually.

  Fire Safety Liaison Gabriel Etcheverry reported that their goal of completing 70
  home wildfire assessments in 2023 was met. He stated restoration of the lights on
  the 20 beacon boxes installed on the east side of Malibu that were damaged by
  tropical storm Hilary was being worked on. He provided an update on the hazard
  tree removal program. He stated that an additional extension of $326,000 to the
  Santa Monica Mountains Conservancy grant was approved and would be brought
  to City Council at the January 8, 2024 meeting. He stated that along with the
  $324,000 initial grant, and previous extension of $350,00, the total was $1,000,000.
  In response to Commissioner Gibbs, he stated that there was demand for hazardous
  tree removal, and they would go through funds quickly if they met their goal of
  removal in the environmentally sensitive habitat areas which included 50
  overgrown palm trees near Kanan Dume Drive. He stated that not all people were
  happy about the removal of the palm trees despite being an invasive species.

  Public Works Director Duboux announced the promotion of Travis Hart to the
  position of Deputy Public Works Director, and stated maintenance items and
  construction were part of his responsibilities. He stated that he was fortunate to
  have his contributions and that the promotion was well-deserved. He provided an
  update on his coordination with Caltrans and stated a meeting was scheduled for
  the following week to examine another section of PCH. He stated that on the
  Caltrans Director’s order, 4.2 million dollars would be introduced for
  improvements and that he would attempt to obtain information on their timeline,
  schedule, and action plan.

  Deputy Public Works Director Hart discussed prior public safety power shutoff
  (PSPS) events and stated that conditions were being monitored and backup
  generators ready for deployment when needed. He reported that the Caltrans

  transfer switch that failed during a PSPS was corrected and should operate properly
  in the future. He reported on upcoming rain events and stated that he monitored
  conditions, along with a consultant and Public Works Director DuBoux. He stated
  that storm drains, inlets, and culverts were clear and maintained in preparation for
  the El Niño season. He reported on sign replacement, storm drain repair, vegetation

  trash receptacles. He reported on capital improvement projects, which included the

  In response to Chair Frost, Deputy Public Works Director Hart stated that they were

  due to the summer construction moratorium on PCH.

  Public Works Director DuBoux stated that some construction was right up against
  houses, so the construction and noise had to be balanced.

  Deputy Public Works Director Hart stated that the project was progressing well,
  and the first stretch was from Topanga Canyon Road to Tuna Canyon Road and
  would continue westward toward John Taylor Drive. He stated that they might have
  to go back and forth on sections due to supply issues and weather conditions.

  In response to Chair Frost, Deputy Public Works Director Hart stated that work
  would likely be done on one side of the highway at a time, but they were set up for
  both sides, so it could be either or both, possibly on the same day. He stated that
  there was not a set schedule, and progress depended on what was accomplished in
  the days and weeks prior.

  Public Works Director DuBoux stated that it also depended on what was found
  during the preparation work.

  In response to Commissioner Merrick, Deputy Public Works Director Hart stated
  vegetation clearance, dewatering set , and export of material had begun on the Zuma
  bridge underpass. He discussed the underpass and stated that when they maintained
  the underpass, it needed to be properly cleared.

ITEM 2.C.  COMMISSIONER COMMENTS

  Ex Officio Member Woodworth stated that he was pleased with the huge, concerted
  effort by City staff, Sheriff’s Department, other agencies, and community groups
  to improve safety on PCH and the canyons. He thanked Public Works Director
  DuBoux for his efforts to improve safety at the Las Flores intersection. He stated
  that the Community Fire Brigade activities were going well and stated his

  appreciation for the dedication of the Los Angeles County Fire Department, Board
  of Supervisors, and the community. He expressed interest in participation in future
  EOC training exercises.

  In response to Ex Officio Member Woodworth, Public Safety Director Dueñas
  stated that the City used DisasterLAN (DLAN) software for the EOC.

  Commissioner Gibbs stated that he focused on PCH safety activities. He reported
  that the memorial installation at PCH and Webb way would be updated to reflect
  59 people killed on PCH due to the recent fatality. He reported that the Community
  Fire Brigades were beginning community outreach and public awareness efforts in
  two pilot communities and recruitment would take place during the next five
  months, with training expected to begin in late spring or early summer of 2024.

  Commissioner Merrick reported that he observed an increased presence by the
  Sheriff’s Department and CHP and stated that enforcement was key to slowing
  traffic and developing a reputation as a law enforcement city that did not tolerate
  speeding. He stated that there would likely be pushback by residents who
  contributed to the safety problem. He stated that he observed an increase in
  homeless encampments developing in the Zuma Creek area, and expressed concern
  for the safety hazard flooding could cause during the upcoming El Niño weather.

  Chair Frost discussed speeding and stated that as a youth he appeared before
  Commissioner Merrick’s father, a judge, for speeding. He thanked meeting
  attendee Carol Randall for her support over the years and stated that he attended his
  first Public Safety meeting with her 20 years prior. He thanked Los Angeles Sheriff
  Department Sergeant Christopher Soderlund for enforcement coverage on PCH and
  stated that the Deputy Joe Tayas’ patrol car was noticeable and observed a
  significant reduction in the racing he heard at the bottom of Paradise Cove from his

Subject:  Policy Establishing Criteria for Declaring and Terminating a Local
  Emergency During Periods of High Fire Risk

RECOMMENDED ACTION: 1) Review a proposed policy that establishes criteria for
declaring the existence of a local emergency and implementing a program for reducing
the risk of fires associated with individuals living unhoused and engaged in unpermitted
and unregulated camping, and 2) Review a proposed policy that establishes criteria for
terminating the local emergency, and 3) Provide a recommendation to the City Council.

DISCUSSION:  On August 23, 2021, the City Council adopted Resolution No. 21-49
Declaring the Existence of a Local Emergency and Establishing a Program for Reducing
the Risk of Fires Associated with Individuals Living Unhoused and Otherwise Engaged in
Unpermitted and Unregulated Camping (Fire Risk Reduction Program). Not only do
encampment fires that spread to the brush put community members at risk, but individuals
living unhoused in the hillsides are at significant risk of loss of life since they are unlikely
to receive traditional emergency alerts sent through cell phones.

The Fire Risk Reduction Program directed city staff to:

•  Act in collaboration with the City of Malibu Outreach Team (MOT), Los Angeles County
  Sheriff’s Department (LASD), and LASD-Homeless Outreach Services Team (HOST)
  to provide appropriate notification to those individuals living unhoused in hillside areas
  of the potential threat to life and the prohibition in effect; and
•  Act in collaboration with the MOT, LASD, and LASD-HOST to identify homeless
  encampments within the areas designated as Very High Fire Hazard Severity Zone
  (VHFHSZ), provide outreach, and offer available resources; and

  Page 1 of 4
  Agenda Item # 5.A.
 •  Act in collaboration with the MOT, LASD, and LASD-HOST, to ensure that the VHFHSZ
  remains free of homeless encampments while also ensuring these efforts do not
  criminalize individuals living unhoused; and
•  Act in collaboration with LASD Arson Watch during Red Flag events to watch for signs
  of smoke columns and fire and communicate potential wildfire incidents as well as
  unpermitted activity in canyons and VHFHSZ areas.

The emergency was terminated on January 10, 2022, after receiving more than six inches
of rain that brought the Live Fuel Moisture (LFM) up to 90%.

To ensure consistency from year to year, staff recommends that a policy be established
that includes criteria that trigger the need to declare a local emergency and implement the
Fire Risk Reduction Program. This policy should also establish the conditions of when to
terminate the local emergency.

Factors to Consider in Developing a Policy

During the calendar year, most days in the Santa Monica Mountain Range are not
conducive to large fire development and, if ignited, are readily extinguished by local fire
resources. This, however, can change under adverse fuel and weather conditions. LFM,
which is the moisture content of living vegetation, is one indicator of fire risk, and an LFM
of 60% or lower is considered critical. When the LFM reaches this critical level, chaparral
and other fuels burn like dead vegetation.

Another significant factor associated with large fire development are Santa Ana wind
events, which typically occur between September and January. These wind events are
especially dangerous when they meet Red Flag Criteria, foretelling extremely dangerous
fire behavior and significant increases in risk to life and property. When the National
Weather Service issues a Red Flag, it triggers fire departments to augment staffing and
apparatus and focus firefighting tactics on evacuations and structure defense.

Specifically, Red Flag Criteria requires dry fuels (when the LFM is at or below 60% and
10-hour Dead Fuel Moisture is at 3% or less) and any one of the following:

  1. Relative Humidity 15 percent or less with either sustained winds 25 mph or greater
  or frequent gusts 35 mph or greater (duration of 6 hours or more).

  2. Relative humidity 10 percent or less with either sustained winds 15 mph or greater
  or frequent gusts 25 mph or greater (duration of 6 hours or more).

  3. Widespread and/or significant Dry Lightning.

  Page 2 of 4

   4. Other (forecaster discretion) – unusual but significant meteorological and/or fuel
  conditions in coordination with GACC or local agency.

The Santa Monica Mountain Range witnesses dry, windy Red Flag conditions around 5-7
times a year, mostly in the months of October, November, and December. In addition, the
duration of heightened wildfire risk varies each year depending on summer temperatures,
rainfall, and wind. Historically, some of the most devastating fires in Malibu occurred in
October and November, including:
  • Old Topanga Fire (16,468 acres) in November 1993;
  • Calabasas Fire (12,513 acres) in October 1996;
  • Corral Canyon Fire (4,708 acres) in November 2007; and,
  • Woolsey Fire (96,949 acres) in November 2018.

By the end of December, the wildfire risk in Malibu tends to decrease significantly as the
state usually receives rainfall, diminishing the threat of a large wildfire.

Recommended Policy

California Government Code Section 8630 empowers the City Council to proclaim the
existence of a local emergency when there is extreme peril to the safety of persons and
property within the territorial limits of the City. This Code also requires that the governing
body proclaim the termination of the local emergency at the earliest possible date that
conditions warrant.

The following criteria is recommended as a policy for declaring the existence of a local
emergency and implementing the Fire Risk Reduction Program:

  • When the LFM is 65% or less as determined by Los Angeles County Fire
  Department Forestry Division for Santa Monica Mountains Chamise;

The following criteria is recommended as a policy for terminating the existence of a local
emergency:

  • When the City has received a minimum of 2" of recorded rainfall as determined by
  Los Angeles County Department of Public Works Season Total (October 1- May 1)
  for the Big Rock Mesa site; and
  • The Live Fuel Moisture is 80% or greater as determined by Los Angeles County
  Fire Department Forestry Division for Santa Monica Mountains Chamise, and
  • When there is no Fire Weather Watch or Red Flag Warning in the extended
  forecast as determined by National Weather Service California Fire Weather
  Forecast for either the Malibu Coast or Santa Monica Mountains NRA.

  filing criminal charges against juvenile offenders.
